name: Mardi Himal Base Camp
tagline: A ridge walk to the foot of Machhapuchhre, 4,500 m up
meta_description: Mardi Himal Base Camp, about 4,500 m: the ridge trek from Pokhara, High Camp, Machhapuchhre views, best months, permits and how many days you need.
summary: Mardi Himal Base Camp sits at about 4,500 m on a grassy ridge directly below Mardi Himal and the south face of Machhapuchhre. It is reached in 4–5 days from Pokhara on a quieter trail than Annapurna Base Camp, with teahouses up to High Camp at 3,580 m and a long dawn push to the top.
intro: Mardi Himal is the 5,587 m peak that stands in front of Machhapuchhre when you look north from Pokhara, a small shoulder of rock and snow beside the famous Fishtail. The trek to its base camp follows a single long ridge that rises out of the forest east of the Modi Khola. It was opened to trekkers only around 2012, and teahouses have grown along it since, but it remains far quieter than the main Annapurna Base Camp trail and is short enough to fit into a week from Pokhara.

The route starts at Kande, 45 minutes from Pokhara, climbs to Australian Camp and Pothana, then enters thick rhododendron and oak forest to Forest Camp at 2,550 m. Above Low Camp at 2,990 m the trees thin out, and from Badal Danda at 3,210 m the ridge becomes open grass with drops on both sides. High Camp at 3,580 m is the last cluster of lodges. From there trekkers leave at 4 am for the upper viewpoint at about 4,250 m and, if legs and weather allow, the base camp at about 4,500 m.

What makes Mardi Himal special is the angle. Machhapuchhre at 6,993 m is close enough from the upper ridge that you can see the fluting of ice on its south face, with Mardi Himal right above you and Annapurna South and Hiunchuli to the west. Below, the clouds often fill the Modi and Mardi valleys like a sea, a common sight on autumn mornings. Most people descend via Siding village to a jeep road, completing the trip in 6–7 days from Pokhara.
facts: Sleep at High Camp 3,580 m, visit base camp on a day trip
45 min drive to Kande + 3–4 days' walk
Close views of Machhapuchhre, quiet ridge trail, cloud seas

highlights.title: Machhapuchhre at close range
highlights.text: From the upper ridge the south face of Machhapuchhre, 6,993 m, rises less than 8 km away. The mountain has never been legally summited and is closed to climbing, which adds to its presence. At dawn the twin-tipped summit turns orange first, then the light runs down the ice flutes towards the valley.

highlights.title: The open grass ridge above Badal Danda
highlights.text: Badal Danda means cloud ridge, and above 3,200 m the trail runs along a narrow crest with the Mardi Khola valley to the east and the Modi Khola gorge to the west. On autumn mornings both valleys fill with cloud while the ridge stays in sunshine, so you walk above a white sea.

highlights.title: Rhododendron forest to Forest Camp
highlights.text: Between Pothana and Low Camp the trail climbs for hours through moss-hung rhododendron, oak and maple. In March and April the rhododendrons bloom red and pink, and in every season you may hear langur monkeys and the calls of the Himalayan monal, Nepal's national bird, in the undergrowth.

highlights.title: Dawn push from High Camp
highlights.text: Summit day starts in the dark at 4 am. The climb from 3,580 m to the upper viewpoint at about 4,250 m takes 2.5–3 hours on a steep grassy trail, and the base camp is another 1–1.5 hours beyond. Sunrise usually catches you on the ridge with Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Mardi Himal glowing.

highlights.title: Quiet compared with ABC
highlights.text: In October the main Annapurna Base Camp trail can see several hundred trekkers a day pass through Chhomrong. Mardi Himal gets a fraction of that, and High Camp has only a handful of lodges. The trade-off is fewer facilities, but the trail feels like a ridge walk rather than a queue.

highlights.title: Siding village on the way down
highlights.text: Most groups descend the eastern side of the ridge to Siding at about 1,750 m, a Gurung farming village of millet terraces and stone houses where few trekkers stayed until recently. A jeep road links Siding with Pokhara in about 2.5 hours, so the return needs no backtracking.

how_to_reach.text: Drive from Pokhara to Kande, about 25 km and 45 minutes on the Baglung highway, then walk. On the way down, a jeep road links Siding or Lumre with Pokhara in 2–2.5 hours. Kathmandu to Pokhara is about 200 km and 6–8 hours by road.

From Kande: Australian Camp and Forest Camp at 2,550 m in about 6 hours, Low Camp and Badal Danda at 3,210 m next day, High Camp at 3,580 m on day three, then a 4 am start for base camp on day four, returning to Low Camp. Total height gain from Kande is about 2,700 m.

Fly Kathmandu to Pokhara in about 25 minutes; mountain views are best from the right-hand side heading west. There is no airstrip on the ridge. In an emergency, helicopters can land near High Camp in good weather, which is why we insist on insurance with evacuation cover.

where_to_stay: There is no lodge at the base camp itself; everyone sleeps at High Camp, 3,580 m, and walks up and down in a day. High Camp has a small cluster of teahouses with twin rooms, shared toilets and dining rooms heated by a stove in the evening. Lower down, Forest Camp, Low Camp and Badal Danda each have a few lodges, usually simpler than on the Annapurna Base Camp trail. In October and November rooms fill, so we book ahead and keep the group small. Before and after the trek our guests stay in Pokhara, where lakeside hotels range from simple guesthouses to 5-star resorts.
tips: Carry a headtorch with fresh batteries, because the climb from High Camp starts in full darkness around 4 am.
Wear a windproof jacket and gloves on summit morning: the exposed ridge above 4,000 m is often −5 to −10 °C before sunrise in autumn.
Turn back at the upper viewpoint if anyone in the group shows signs of altitude sickness, as the view from 4,250 m is already superb.
Fill water bottles at High Camp, because there is no water source on the upper ridge.
Avoid the trail after fresh snow in winter, when the narrow ridge above Badal Danda becomes slippery and exposed.

experiences.title: Sunrise hike from High Camp to the upper viewpoint
experiences.summary: The defining day of the Mardi Himal trek: a 4 am climb from High Camp at 3,580 m to the upper viewpoint at about 4,250 m and, for those with energy, the base camp at about 4,500 m, timed for first light on Machhapuchhre.
body: Your guide knocks on the door at about 3:45 am. After tea and biscuits the group leaves High Camp in a line of headtorches, following a steep, narrow path up the grassy crest. There are a few exposed sections where the ridge is only a couple of metres wide, and in autumn the frost makes the grass slick, so poles and slow steps help. The first hour is the steepest. By the time the sky starts to grey, most groups are close to the top of the first rise.

The upper viewpoint at about 4,250 m is where many trekkers stop. It looks straight onto the south face of Machhapuchhre and up to Mardi Himal, with Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and the long wall of the Annapurna massif to the west. If the weather is clear and everyone feels well, the trail continues across rougher ground to the base camp at about 4,500 m, a further 1–1.5 hours. There are no buildings, just stones, prayer flags and the peaks.

The descent is where the day becomes long. From the base camp it is about 3 hours back to High Camp for a late breakfast, then another 2–3 hours down to Low Camp at 2,990 m, where we sleep to recover. Total walking can reach 9 hours. Carry 2 litres of water, snacks, sunscreen and a warm layer, as the sun is fierce once it clears the ridge and the wind picks up after 10 am.

faqs.q: Do I have to go all the way to Mardi Himal Base Camp?
faqs.a: No. Many trekkers turn around at the upper viewpoint at about 4,250 m, which already gives the full close view of Machhapuchhre and Mardi Himal. Continuing to the base camp at about 4,500 m adds 2–3 hours return over rougher ground. Your guide will judge on the day based on weather, time and how everyone is coping with the altitude.

faqs.q: How cold is it at the Mardi Himal viewpoint at dawn?
faqs.a: In October and November expect around −5 to −10 °C before sunrise, colder with wind chill on the ridge. In March and April it is usually a few degrees warmer. Wear a down jacket, a hat, warm gloves and a buff, and keep your phone battery in an inside pocket, because cold drains it quickly and you will want photos at first light.

faqs.q: Is the ridge to Mardi Himal Base Camp dangerous?
faqs.a: In good conditions it is a steep but non-technical walk. The risk comes from frost, ice or fresh snow on the narrow sections and from strong wind later in the morning. We do not go up after heavy snowfall, we start early so the descent happens before the worst wind, and the guide decides the turnaround point. Good boots and poles make a real difference.

experiences.title: Rhododendron forest walk to Forest Camp
experiences.best_time: March–April for blooms, Oct–Nov for clear skies
experiences.summary: The first full day on the Mardi Himal trail climbs from Pothana into an old forest of rhododendron, oak and maple, reaching Forest Camp at 2,550 m. In spring the canopy blooms red and pink; in autumn it is cool, quiet and full of birdsong.
body: After the open hillside of Australian Camp and the tea shops of Pothana, the trail to Forest Camp turns into the trees and stays there for most of the day. This is a mature mid-hill forest dominated by Rhododendron arboreum, Nepal's national flower, which can grow into trees 15 m tall. Mixed in are oaks, maples and magnolias draped with moss and ferns. The path is a mix of earth and roots, gently but steadily climbing about 550 m over 5–6 hours from Kande.

Wildlife is easier to hear than see. Grey langur monkeys move through the canopy, and if you walk quietly in the early morning you may spot kalij pheasants or a Himalayan monal in the clearings. Birders should listen for laughingthrushes and sunbirds near the flowering rhododendrons in spring. Leeches appear in the monsoon months, which is one reason we do not run this trek from June to August. Binoculars add little weight and help a great deal here.

Forest Camp, also called Kokar, is a small clearing with a few lodges. It feels remote after the busy road head at Kande, and on clear evenings you can see the light fading on Machhapuchhre through gaps in the trees. In March and April the blooms are at their best between roughly 2,500 m and 3,200 m, which puts this section and the climb to Low Camp in the heart of the flowering zone.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom on the Mardi Himal trek?
faqs.a: Usually from mid-March to late April, moving uphill as the season warms. The lower forest near Pothana flowers first, and by April the blooms reach Low Camp and Badal Danda at around 3,000–3,200 m. Exact timing varies with each year's winter, so a late cold spell can delay them by two or three weeks.

faqs.q: Are there leeches on the way to Forest Camp?
faqs.a: Only in the wet months. From June to September the damp forest between Pothana and Low Camp has many leeches, which is one reason we do not sell this trek in the monsoon. In October to May they are rare. If you do walk in the rains, wear long socks over your trousers and carry salt or anti-leech spray.

faqs.q: Is the Forest Camp section suitable for beginners?
faqs.a: Yes. It is the gentlest full day of the trek, climbing about 550 m over 5–6 hours on a shaded path without exposure. Beginners with reasonable fitness manage it comfortably if they keep a steady pace. The harder days come later, especially the climb from High Camp to the viewpoint, so use this day to find your rhythm.

experiences.title: Descent to Siding, a quiet Gurung farm village
experiences.summary: Rather than retrace the ridge, our Mardi Himal treks drop east from Low Camp to Siding at about 1,750 m, a Gurung village of millet terraces and stone houses, then drive back to Pokhara. It is a steep knee-testing descent with a welcome cultural finish.
body: From Low Camp at 2,990 m a narrower trail leaves the main ridge and dives east through forest towards the Mardi Khola valley. It loses about 1,250 m in 3–4 hours, and parts are steep with loose soil and roots, so poles are useful and knees should be kept soft. The forest gives way to bamboo, then to the first terraces, and the sound of the river grows louder below.

Siding is a farming village rather than a trekking hub. Families grow millet, maize and potatoes on the terraces, keep buffalo and goats, and a few houses have begun to offer homestay rooms and simple meals. Lunch here is often dal bhat cooked over a wood fire with greens from the garden. Children walk to school along the same paths, and older women may be weaving bamboo baskets on their verandas.

A jeep road now reaches Siding and the neighbouring village of Lumre, and the drive back to Pokhara takes about 2–2.5 hours down the Mardi Khola valley. The road is rough and can be blocked after heavy rain, so in the shoulder seasons we keep the option of walking further down to a better road head. By late afternoon most groups are back at Phewa Lake, which makes this a neat way to close the trek.

faqs.q: Is the descent from Low Camp to Siding steep?
faqs.a: Yes, it is the steepest descent on the trek, losing about 1,250 m in 3–4 hours on a narrow forest path. It can be slippery after rain and dusty in spring. Walking poles take much of the strain off your knees, and good boots with ankle support help. Go slowly; there is no hurry once the summit day is behind you.

faqs.q: Can we stay overnight in Siding?
faqs.a: Yes. A few households in Siding now offer homestay rooms with simple meals, and staying adds a relaxed cultural night before you drive back to Pokhara. Facilities are basic, often with shared toilets and no heating. We can arrange it as an extra night on our Mardi Himal trek if you would like more time in the village.

faqs.q: How long is the drive from Siding to Pokhara?
faqs.a: About 2–2.5 hours by jeep on a rough dirt road down the Mardi Khola valley before joining paved roads near Pokhara. The road can close after heavy rain, especially in June to September and occasionally in spring storms, so your guide will check conditions the day before and arrange an alternative pick-up point if needed.

faqs.q: How high is Mardi Himal Base Camp?
faqs.a: Mardi Himal Base Camp sits at about 4,500 m, though published figures range from roughly 4,400 m to 4,500 m because there is no single marked point. The upper viewpoint, where many trekkers stop, is at about 4,250 m. Mardi Himal peak itself is 5,587 m, and High Camp, the last place with lodges, is at 3,580 m.

faqs.q: How many days is the Mardi Himal trek?
faqs.a: Most itineraries take 4–5 walking days from Kande and back to a road head at Siding, so 6–7 days from Pokhara including arrival and departure. Our standard trip is 7 days from Pokhara. Add 2 days if you start and finish in Kathmandu, or allow one extra day at High Camp if you want a second chance at a clear summit morning.

faqs.q: Is the Mardi Himal trek difficult?
faqs.a: We grade it Moderate. Daily walking is 4–6 hours, except summit day, which can run to 9 hours with a 4 am start and a gain of about 900 m to the base camp before a long descent. The trail is steep in places and narrow on the upper ridge, but not technical. Regular hikers with good fitness manage it well.

faqs.q: Mardi Himal or Annapurna Base Camp, which is better?
faqs.a: Choose Mardi Himal if you have about a week, want a quieter trail and love ridge walking with close views of Machhapuchhre. Choose Annapurna Base Camp if you have 10–12 days and want to stand inside the Annapurna Sanctuary, ringed by 7,000 m and 8,000 m peaks. ABC has more lodges and more people; Mardi has fewer of both.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Mardi Himal?
faqs.a: Yes. The trek lies in the Annapurna Conservation Area, so you need an ACAP permit: NPR 3,000 for foreigners and NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals, including Indians. Since 2023 Nepal's rules require foreign trekkers in conservation areas to walk with a licensed guide, though enforcement has varied. Check current status before you travel; our packages include the permit and a licensed guide.

faqs.q: What is the best time for Mardi Himal trek?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest skies and the most reliable views from the upper ridge. March and April bring rhododendron blooms below 3,200 m but hazier afternoons. December to February is possible with cold mornings and occasional snow on the ridge. We avoid June to August because of rain, leeches and cloud that hides Machhapuchhre for days.

faqs.q: Are there teahouses at Mardi Himal Base Camp?
faqs.a: No. The last lodges are at High Camp, 3,580 m, and everyone visits the base camp as a day trip. Some years a seasonal tea stall operates near the upper viewpoint, but do not rely on it. Carry water, snacks and warm clothes for the full day. Forest Camp, Low Camp, Badal Danda and High Camp all have small teahouses.

faqs.q: Can beginners do the Mardi Himal trek?
faqs.a: Fit beginners can, provided they walk regularly at home and are comfortable with long climbs. The first three days are steady forest and ridge walking. Summit day is the real test because of the early start, altitude and long descent. Beginners can stop at the upper viewpoint, which still gives the best of the views, and save energy for the way down.

faqs.q: How much does the Mardi Himal trek cost from Pokhara?
faqs.a: Our 7-day Mardi Himal trek from Pokhara starts from about ₹45,000 or US$530 per person, twin sharing, with guide, porter support, permits, teahouse rooms, three meals a day on the trail and road transfers. Independent trekkers spend roughly US$30–40 a day on food and rooms, plus the ACAP permit. Prices rise in peak October and November.
